query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In the as‐built AM Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy, the degradation during prolonged high‐temperature exposure is governed by the evolution and integrity of a Cr/Al‐rich oxide scale that forms preferentially along the high-density grain boundaries and other AM-induced defects. This oxide scale, which forms under oxidizing atmospheres, builds up internal stresses during growth that eventually lead to spallation and interfacial debonding; in reducing environments, insufficient protective scale formation allows for accelerated internal oxidation and embrittlement, ultimately triggering catastrophic failure.
generation.material_initial_state: Additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an FCC matrix exhibiting a high density of grain boundaries and residual stresses that stem from the rapid solidification inherent to the AM process.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled post-build annealing treatment aimed at reducing the grain-boundary density and relieving internal stresses. This is coupled with exposing samples to either oxidizing or reducing atmospheres under identical high-temperature conditions.
generation.conditions: Expose both as-built and annealed samples to temperatures in the range of 750–850°C for extended durations (e.g., several hundred hours) under well-controlled gas atmospheres—one with an oxidizing nature (such as air or an oxygen-enriched blend) and another with a reducing character (e.g., a H2/Ar mixture).
generation.structural_mediator: The morphology and adhesion of the Cr/Al-enriched oxide scale at alloy grain boundaries and defects.
generation.mechanism: High-density grain boundaries in the as-built material accelerate localized oxidation. Under oxidizing conditions, this leads to the rapid formation and subsequent growth of a brittle oxide scale that generates high internal stresses and eventually spalls off, while under reducing conditions the limited scale formation permits internal oxidation and embrittlement. Both pathways compromise the structural integrity and lead to catastrophic failure.
generation.predicted_outcome: If the hypothesis is correct, the annealed samples (with reduced grain-boundary density and relieved residual stress) will exhibit slower or more uniform oxide scale growth, reduced scale spallation, and therefore improved mechanical performance relative to the as-built baseline. Moreover, the contrasting behaviors between oxidizing (where spallation of an overly thick, stressed, oxide scale dominates) and reducing (where lack of protective scale leads to internal oxidation) environments will confirm the key role of oxide scale evolution in governing degradation.
generation.baseline: The as-built additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy without post-build annealing treatment.
generation.boundary: Applicable within the temperature regime of 750–850°C and under atmospheres that distinctly favor oxidation versus reduction; the observed failure modes are assessed before complete material degradation (i.e., prior to total loss of mechanical integrity).
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative rates of oxide scale growth and the critical stress thresholds for spallation are uncertain due to variability in the AM-induced defect distribution and scale adhesion kinetics. The precise balance of oxidation versus internal diffusion under different gas environments may also vary.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set in the as-built condition and another set subjected to a controlled annealing treatment to reduce grain-boundary density. Expose both sets to 800°C under two separate atmospheres—an oxidizing environment (e.g., air or oxygen-rich) and a reducing environment (e.g., H2/Ar mixture). At predetermined time intervals (e.g., every 100 hours), remove samples for detailed characterization.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness, composition, and integrity via SEM/EDS and XRD
Interfacial adhesion strength through micro-mechanical testing
Grain-boundary density and residual stress analysis pre- and post-anneal
Mechanical performance assessments (tensile or creep tests)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the post-annealed samples do not show a measurable improvement (i.e., reduced oxide scale spallation, slower oxide scale growth, and better mechanical integrity) compared to the as-built alloy, or if changing the gas atmosphere (oxidizing vs. reducing) does not yield contrasting degradation behaviors, then the hypothesis that grain-boundary-mediated oxidation governs the failure mechanism is falsified.
